content.title: About
content.content: Sweet and sour pork is a classic Chinese dish made from bite‑size pieces of pork coated in a light batter, deep‑fried, and tossed in a sauce of vinegar, sugar, soy sauce, ketchup and spices. The dish combines a crunchy texture with a bright sweet‑sour flavor and is enjoyed worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the Canton region in the 19th century as a way to balance sweet and sour tastes typical of the local cuisine.
Traditional recipes include pineapple, bell pepper and carrot, though many modern versions simplify the ingredient list.
In the United States the dish became widely popular after being featured on the menu of Panda Express in the 1980s.
The sauce is usually made from a blend of rice or apple cider vinegar, sugar, ketchup and corn starch for thickening.
Sweet and sour pork is often served with steamed rice or noodles to temper the bold sauce.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable content
items.content: Traditional additions like bell pepper, carrot and pineapple add vitamin C and dietary fiber.

items.title: Moderate fat when prepared wisely
items.content: Using lean cuts of pork and limiting oil can make the dish fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Antioxidants in the sauce
items.content: Tomatoes and vinegar contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sauce often contains a lot of sugar, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Soy sauce and vinegar add salt, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy sauce may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Pork must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella and trichinella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, straight from the wok, with steamed rice, noodles or a vegetable side. Garnish with fresh cilantro or sliced green onions for extra aroma. To reduce sweetness, cut back on sugar or substitute with honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a splash of water to keep the sauce from drying out. The dish can be frozen for up to 2 months after it has cooled completely.
